title: Early intervention in psychosis: peer support feasibility study, prose scan reply refused, cited feasibility trial corrected after a late acceptance
notes: Adversarial path on a clear feasibility study (the need names a feasibility study and interviews; classifyFamily gives feasibility, explicit). A fixture search returns six records. The first scan reply is prose, not JSON: nothing is applied, an error is shown, the records stay unrated and the stage stays incomplete (G5). A valid second call (shape appraisal) annotates the six records and records claims c1 to c4. The Design stage recommends feasibility and proposes a decision resting on claims c2 to c4, with one gate met (funded posts) and one unknown (approvals). The investigator reads the protocol and statistics drafts first and accepts the decision afterwards on the Design panel (accepted, blocked). Then the key findings of the feasibility trial behind claim c2 are corrected through the store: the decision must become stale in the store, on screen, after reload and in the export, and every completed stage after Scan, including protocol and stats, is flagged for review; the later stages completed afterwards are not. The problem reply restates the typed constraints verbatim, so G11 is not engaged. Record ids are stableRecordId(record) from src/lib/evidence/records.ts, computed by the generator: DOI-based for records 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 (ev-1g96e5y, ev-086u53q, ev-15dq183, ev-05nkrf7, ev-0hehrv4) and title and year for record 4 (ev-1mngnqj). Requires S13 (appraisal dispatch), S10 (evidence revision covering keyFindings; amendment A3.2 D24 names the same defect), S11 (selectionStatus, actionStatus) and D5 (status text). inputs.need:
I am a consultant psychiatrist and clinical lead of an early intervention in psychosis team that looks after about 210 young people aged 14 to 35 in their first three years after a first episode. Too many of them drift away from the service in the first year, especially young men, people using cannabis and people without stable housing, and families tell us that what helped most was meeting someone who had been through it. The trust's innovation fund has now agreed to pay for two part-time peer support workers, people with their own experience of psychosis, for twelve months from January 2027.

I want to run a feasibility study alongside their introduction, so that we learn whether a proper trial of peer support in our service would be possible and worth doing. The things I do not know are whether young people will take up the offer, whether they stay in contact, whether the peer workers can do the role as intended without burning out, and whether we can collect outcome questionnaires without adding appointments. I would also like interviews with young people, families and staff about how the role works in practice, and a clear set of criteria for deciding whether to go on to a trial.

We have no research funding beyond the peer worker posts, and the evaluation must rely on routinely collected data plus short questionnaires. Some of the young people are under 18. The trust's research and development office has not looked at the plan yet, and I am not sure what approvals we need.
inputs.constraints: Peer support worker posts funded for 12 months from January 2027; no other research funding. Evaluation uses routine data and short questionnaires only; no extra appointments for service users. Some participants are aged 14 to 17.

records.title: Peer support for people with early psychosis: a systematic review
records.authors: Kinsella-Obi R, Marchand-Asante L, Petrova-Hale D
records.venue: Early Intervention in Mental Health Reviews
records.abstract: We included nine studies of peer support for people within five years of a first episode of psychosis, two of them randomised. Peer support was associated with better engagement with services and higher scores on hope and recovery measures, but there was no clear effect on readmission or symptoms. Definitions of the peer role varied widely, from one-to-one mentoring to group facilitation, and few studies described training or supervision. Most studies were small and short, and only three reported how many eligible people took up the offer.

records.title: Peer support workers in early intervention services for psychosis: a randomised feasibility trial
records.authors: Adeyemi-Lindqvist S, Harcourt-Nakamura J, Osei-Brennan T
records.abstract: In two early intervention teams we aimed to randomise 80 young people to peer support plus usual care or usual care alone over 12 months. We recruited 64 participants, and 78 percent provided six-month outcome data. Participants allocated to peer support had a median of 1.8 contacts a week with their peer worker. Recovery questionnaires were completed by 70 percent at six months, lower among participants under 18. The trial met its progression criteria for recruitment and retention and was judged feasible for a definitive trial.

records.title: Role clarity, supervision and turnover among peer support workers in community mental health teams: a mixed-methods study
records.abstract: We surveyed 118 peer support workers and interviewed 24 in community mental health teams. Forty percent of those surveyed had left their post within a year, most often citing unclear roles, being asked to do administrative work and lack of supervision from someone with lived experience. Workers with protected supervision and a written role description stayed longer. Several described distress when working with people whose experiences echoed their own. The study was cross-sectional, so causes of turnover cannot be separated from features of the teams.

records.title: Disengagement from early intervention in psychosis services: rates and predictors in a regional cohort
records.abstract: Among 1,102 young people accepted by four early intervention services, 23 percent disengaged within 12 months, defined as no contact for three months despite attempts. Disengagement was more common among young men, people using cannabis daily and people without stable housing, and less common when a family member was involved in care. Most disengagement happened in the first six months. Reasons were recorded for only a third of those who disengaged, and the study could not assess which service features protected against it.

records.title: What young people and families want from peer support in early psychosis: interviews in three services
records.abstract: We interviewed 27 young people and 14 family members from three early intervention services. Young people valued meeting someone who had lived through psychosis and come out the other side, and preferred flexible contact by text or in community places rather than clinic rooms. Families welcomed practical advice on navigating services. Some young people worried that a peer worker would pass information to the clinical team, and some families felt excluded when contact was one-to-one. Participants asked for clear rules on confidentiality before starting.

records.title: Brief recovery and hope questionnaires in early psychosis: completion rates and responsiveness
records.abstract: We examined completion and responsiveness of three brief recovery and hope questionnaires given at routine reviews in early intervention services. Completion was 74 percent at baseline and 58 percent at six months, lowest among young people under 18 and those who had missed reviews. The shortest questionnaire was completed most often and detected change as well as the longer ones. Completion rose when a named worker asked in person rather than by post. We recommend the shortest questionnaire for routine use.

steps.responseText: Thank you for sharing the records. Peer support in early psychosis is a promising and growing area. Taken together, the studies you retrieved suggest that peer support workers can improve engagement and hope, that feasibility trials in similar teams have recruited reasonably well, and that peer workers themselves need clear roles and supervision to stay in post. Disengagement in the first year is common, and questionnaire completion falls among younger participants. I would recommend a feasibility study with progression criteria covering recruitment, retention, delivery and questionnaire completion. If it would help, I can set this out as a structured appraisal with ratings for each study and a list of claims linked to the evidence.

response.synthesis: Six retrieved records, appraised at abstract level after the first reply arrived as prose and was not applied. Peer support in early psychosis is associated with better engagement and hope but not with fewer readmissions. A randomised feasibility trial in two teams recruited most of its target and retained most participants, giving benchmarks for progression criteria. Peer workers leave often when roles are unclear, a quarter of young people disengage within a year, and questionnaire completion falls among under-18s unless someone asks in person.
response.gradeRationale: One moderate-quality feasibility trial and otherwise small observational and qualitative studies; consistent in direction for engagement but imprecise and from few services.
